passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel a story of two sisters, daughters of one mother, who were unfaithful from their youth in Egypt. ‘The older was named Oholah, and her sister was named Oholibah. They became Mine and gave birth to sons and daughters. As for their identities, Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem’ (verse 4).

Oholah gave herself to the Assyrians, their splendid officers and horsemen, and took up their idols (verses 5-8). ‘Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, the Assyrians for whom she lusted’ (verse 9), and they destroyed her. ‘Her sister Oholibah saw this, yet in her lust and prostitution she was more depraved than her sister’ (verse 11). She turned to the Assyrians and then to the Babylonians, whose officers she saw painted on walls, and then to Egypt (verses 12-21). The chapter tells this in coarse sexual language, which these notes name and do not repeat.
passages.hearers:
The chapter compresses about three centuries of foreign policy. The northern kingdom, with its capital at Samaria, bought Assyria's favor again and again; King Menahem paid a heavy tribute to the king called Pul. When the north turned to Egypt, Assyria besieged Samaria, and it fell in 722 BC. Judah followed the same road. Ahaz sent temple silver to Assyria, Hezekiah showed his treasures to Babylon's envoys, and Judah's last kings swung between Babylon and Egypt.

Treaties were religious as well as political. A vassal swore oaths in the names of the overlord's gods and often honored them, which is why seeking an empire's protection and taking up its idols go together. Both names come from the Hebrew for tent; the usual explanation is her own tent, and God's tent in her, perhaps contrasting the north's own shrines with the LORD's sanctuary in Jerusalem, though that is not certain.

The language is deliberately coarse. Ezekiel wanted his hearers, the male elders of the exile, to feel disgust at what they had come to call sensible statecraft.
passages.later: Jeremiah told the same story of two unfaithful sisters: ‘Yet that unfaithful sister Judah had no fear’ (Jeremiah 3:8). Assyria ‘captured Samaria and carried away the Israelites to Assyria’ (2 Kings 17:6).
passages.asks: Oholibah watched what happened to her sister and went further. Ask what warnings you have seen in others' lives and ignored. And ask where you are running to some other power for safety.

passages.t: The lovers turned against her, and her sister's cup
passages.happening:
‘I will incite your lovers against you’ (verse 22). God will bring the Babylonians and all the Assyrians against Jerusalem from every side, with chariots and weapons, and they will judge her by their own standards (verses 23-24). The verses that follow picture what conquering armies did to captured cities and their people; these notes name it and do not describe it (verses 25-29).

‘You will drink your sister’s cup, a cup deep and wide’ (verse 32), ‘a cup of devastation and desolation, the cup of your sister Samaria’ (verse 33). ‘Because you have forgotten Me and have cast Me behind your back, you must bear the consequences of your indecency and prostitution’ (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
The lovers are the empires. The punishment is what they will do to Jerusalem when they turn on her: the siege, the plunder, the killing and the captivity that ancient armies carried out on cities they took. Ezekiel draws on the brutal treatment of captives in war and on ancient penalties for adultery to describe the coming disaster.

The cup is a common prophetic picture of judgment, a drink that brings staggering and ruin. Jerusalem will drink the same cup that Samaria drank in 722 BC.
passages.later: Isaiah called Jerusalem to awake, ‘you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury’ (Isaiah 51:17). Jeremiah was told to make the nations drink the cup of God's wrath (Jeremiah 25:15).
passages.hard:
How should a reader handle this chapter's sexual imagery and its violence against a woman's body?

Many readers find this chapter, with chapter 16, among the most disturbing in the Bible, and the difficulty should be admitted plainly. It pictures a nation as a woman, describes her in explicit terms, and depicts her stripping and death as God's judgment. Some interpreters, among them feminist scholars, argue that it sexualizes violence and has been used to excuse abuse.

These verses are a picture of two cities and a covenant. The woman is a nation, and the first hearers were the male elders and leaders of Israel; the shock was aimed at men who were being told that their proud foreign policy was the conduct of a faithless wife. The violence described is what conquering armies actually did to captured cities, their women and their children; the prophet is describing the coming disaster in the terms of its brutal reality, not prescribing how anyone should treat a woman. Interpreters weigh the picture differently, some reading it as rhetoric of alarm whose excess is part of its warning, others calling for it to be read critically and with lament. All agree that using this chapter to justify the mistreatment of women is a grave misuse.

So it must be said plainly. This is a prophetic picture of God and two cities. It gives no warrant for any man to shame, strip, threaten or harm a wife, or anyone, and no one may use it to say that a woman deserves to be hurt.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jerusalem's ruin began when she forgot God and cast him behind her back. Ask what in your life you have pushed behind you so that you do not have to look at it. And ask what it would mean to turn and face God again.

passages.happening:
God asks Ezekiel to judge Oholah and Oholibah and confront them with their abominations (verse 36). Now the picture gives way to the plain charges. ‘They have committed adultery with their idols. They have even sacrificed their children, whom they bore to Me, in the fire as food for their idols’ (verse 37). ‘On the very day they slaughtered their children for their idols, they entered My sanctuary to profane it. Yes, they did this inside My house’ (verse 39).

They sent for foreign envoys and dressed themselves to receive them (verses 40-44). Righteous men will judge them, and God will put an end to their idolatry in the land (verses 45-48). ‘Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD’ (verse 49).
passages.hearers:
The last section names the literal sins behind the metaphor: idolatry, child sacrifice, and profaning the temple and the Sabbath. What horrified Ezekiel most was that people came from killing their children for idols straight into God's house, as if nothing had happened.

The warning in verse 48 belongs to the same picture of judgment on a nation's idolatry. It gives no one a warrant to shame or harm any woman.
passages.later: Jeremiah condemned the high places of Topheth, where people burned their sons and daughters, ‘something I never commanded’ (Jeremiah 7:31). The law forbade giving children to Molech (Leviticus 18:21).
passages.asks: The people came from their idols straight into God's house. Ask where your worship on Sunday and your life during the week have come apart. And ask what it would mean to bring them back together.
